title: John 1:1 — 'the Word was a god'
claim: The New World Translation renders John 1:1c 'and the Word was a god,' against virtually every major English translation (KJV, NIV, ESV, NASB, NRSV, even the Catholic NAB), which all read 'the Word was God.' Bruce Metzger of Princeton called it 'a frightful mistranslation' — 'erroneous,' 'pernicious,' 'reprehensible' (Theology Today, April 1953). The rendering serves the Watchtower's denial of Christ's deity, yet it creates a problem their own theology can't absorb: if the Word is 'a god' alongside Jehovah, the NWT teaches a second, lesser god — while Jehovah says 'before me there was no God formed, and after me there continued to be none' (NWT Isaiah 43:10). Watchtower literature defends the rendering by citing the absence of the Greek definite article before theos, and by appealing to a handful of obscure translations. The indefinite rendering also collides with John's own usage: anarthrous theos appears in John 1:6, 12, 13, 18, where the NWT renders 'God.'

The editorial history is damning: the 1950 edition printed 'other' with no brackets; after criticism, later editions bracketed it ('all [other] things') to mark it as an addition; the 2013 revision removed the brackets again, so current readers cannot see the word is not in the Greek. The same maneuver is not applied at Romans 8:38-39 or John 1:3, where 'all things' is left alone — the insertion appears exactly where Christology is at stake.

title: Hebrews 1:8 — 'God is your throne'
claim: Hebrews 1:8, quoting Psalm 45:6, is traditionally rendered 'But of the Son he says, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever' — the Father addressing the Son as God. Notably, verse 10 goes on to apply Psalm 102 — words addressed to YHWH about creating heavens and earth — directly to the Son, which the NWT translates straightforwardly.

title: Luke 23:43 — the relocated comma
claim: To the thief on the cross, Jesus says (all major translations): 'Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.' The NWT moves the comma: 'Truly I tell you today, you will be with me in paradise' — Jesus is merely saying it today, promising paradise at some unspecified future point. The relocation protects two Watchtower doctrines at once: soul sleep (the thief cannot be conscious anywhere that day) and a two-class afterlife (the thief belongs to the earthly-paradise class, not heaven). The pattern evidence is strong: forms of 'truly I say to you' occur over 70 times in the Gospels, and in no other instance does a time adverb attach to the saying formula rather than the content. The earliest manuscripts, however, carry virtually no punctuation, so the comma is in every translation an editorial decision — the question is whose decision follows the evidence and whose follows doctrine.

title: DON'T USE: 'The 2024 Changes Ended Shunning'

They wore the purple triangle in the camps, and the survivor literature — including from Jewish survivors — repeatedly describes them as the prisoners least likely to inform and most likely to share food. In the United States they litigated their way to the Supreme Court more than fifty times between 1938 and 1955, and the case law they won belongs to everyone: West Virginia v. Barnette (1943) established that no American can be compelled to salute a flag or profess a belief, and Cantwell v. Connecticut (1940) applied the Free Exercise Clause to the states. Much of the religious-liberty protection every American church now relies on was bought by Jehovah's Witnesses in court. Russia banned the organization as 'extremist' in 2017 and has imprisoned members since; the persecution is not only historical.
